title: An Orphan Becomes Queen of Persia
overview: The king gathers young women to replace Vashti, and Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, is chosen as queen while Mordecai quietly saves the king's life.

parts.label: Searching for a new queen (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Once the king's anger cooled, his attendants proposed gathering young women from every province into his harem, with his favorite replacing Vashti. The women were taken by royal order, not invited, so they had no real choice in the matter.

parts.label: Mordecai and Esther (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: Mordecai is a Jewish man in Susa whose family had been deported from Jerusalem by Babylon, and his ancestor Kish shares a name with King Saul's father, which may set up the clash with Haman in the next chapter. He raised his orphaned cousin as his daughter; her Hebrew name Hadassah means myrtle, and Esther may come from a word for star, though scholars are not certain.

parts.label: Taken into the palace (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: Esther was brought in with many others, and Hegai, the court official in charge of the women, gave her special care, food and the best rooms. On Mordecai's instruction she hid that she was Jewish, and he walked by the harem courtyard every day for news of her, since outsiders could not go in.

parts.label: A year of preparation (vv. 12-14)
parts.note: Each woman spent twelve months in beauty treatments, then one night with the king. Afterward she lived in a separate house among his secondary wives, likely unable to marry anyone else, and saw him again only if he called her by name.

parts.label: Esther is crowned (vv. 15-20)
parts.note: Esther took only what Hegai advised, and in the king's seventh year, about four years after Vashti was removed, he crowned her queen with a feast and gifts to the provinces, possibly tax relief or pardons. She still kept her people secret and followed Mordecai's guidance as she had growing up.

parts.label: Mordecai stops a plot (vv. 21-23)
parts.note: Sitting at the king's gate probably means Mordecai held some official post, and there he learned that two guards planned to kill the king. He told Esther, the men were executed on a wooden pole or stake (translations differ on the exact method), and his deed went into the royal records, which matters later in the story.

disagreement: Since God is never named in Esther, Christians differ over whether to read her rise mainly as God's hidden hand quietly arranging events or as a more human story of surviving and making hard choices inside an unjust system.
think: When someone has very little control over what happens to them, how do you think their choices within those limits should be judged?
